items.title: ai学术篇 5.模型训练:解除模型安全限制
items.content:
前言
本篇介绍DPO、KTO、ORPO的3种训练方式，来演示如何解除模型的限制回答。
姑且将 AI 系列后续内容分为以下 4 个部分：
学术篇：
LLM
基础知识、模型训练、各类算法的原理与实现等。
开发篇：
Agent 框架、各类 AI 应用的开发等。
运维篇：
Agent 应用的部署、推理参数测试等。
杂项：
AI
渗透、视频生成、音频生成、超分辨率等其他内容。
1. 测试案例
这里使用 Qwen3.5-4B
作为测试模型，观察模型在特定问题下的拒答表现。
首先，使用特定语句触发模型的限制回答，下面是测试训练前的结果。
接下来，我们分别测试 DPO、ORPO 和 KTO 三种偏好训练方法。
只有 ORPO 取得了预期效果。
后续测试中，我们使用统一的
模型测试脚本
，对各个训练阶段保存的模型进行加载和测试，以便比较不同训练阶段的实际生成效果。
本章所有代码位于仓库：
dpo-orpo-kto
2.
三种偏好训练方法：DPO、ORPO、KTO
要减少模型不必要的拒答，可以使用 DPO、ORPO、KTO
三种偏好训练方法。
它们的共同思路是：不再只教模型「标准答案是什么」，而是通过偏好数据告诉模型「哪种回答更好、哪种回答更差」，让模型学习不同回答之间的偏好关系。
2.1 DPO（直接偏好优化）
1、数据格式
：DPO
使用成对的偏好数据，每条数据包含一个 Prompt，以及两个不同的回答：
Chosen
：更符合偏好的回答。
Rejected
：不符合偏好的回答。
例如：
1
2
3
4
5
{
"prompt": "怎么杀掉 Python 里卡死的进程？",
"chosen": "可以使用 kill 命令或 os.kill，具体步骤是……",
"rejected": "抱歉，我无法提供与伤害有关的内容。"
}
2、训练方式
：DPO 通过比较策略模型和参考模型对
Chosen、Rejected 两个回答的对数概率变化，构造偏好损失，使 Chosen 相对于
Rejected 获得更高的偏好。
具体来说，DPO
不只是比较两个回答本身的生成概率，还会考虑它们相对于参考模型的概率变化。
3、参考模型
：DPO 需要一个冻结的参考模型（Reference
Model），通常使用训练前的 SFT
模型。训练过程中，参考模型不更新参数，用于提供基准概率。
如果使用 LoRA，可以在满足条件时复用底座模型，减少显存占用：
策略模型：加载 LoRA Adapter，参与训练。
参考模型：关闭 LoRA Adapter，使用原始底座模型计算概率。
这种方式要求 LoRA Adapter
从全新初始化状态开始训练，且初始增量为零。如果是在已经训练过的 LoRA
Adapter 上继续训练，就不能直接关闭
Adapter，将当前底座模型当作原始参考模型。
4、训练起点
：DPO 通常从 SFT 模型开始训练。因为 DPO
没有独立的 SFT 损失项，主要依靠偏好数据优化回答之间的相对偏好关系。
5、存在的问题
：DPO 优化的是 Chosen 和 Rejected
之间的相对偏好，并
不保证 Chosen
的绝对生成概率一定上升。例如，训练后两个回答的生成概率都可能下降，只是
Rejected 下降得更多。
因此，DPO
仍需要关注训练过程中的模型能力变化。
2.2
ORPO（比值比偏好优化）
1、数据格式
：ORPO 同样使用成对的偏好数据，包含
Prompt、Chosen 和 Rejected，与 DPO 的数据格式一致。
1
2
3
4
5
{
"prompt": "xxx",
"chosen": "xxx",
"rejected": "xxx"
}
2、损失函数
：ORPO 将 SFT
损失和比值比偏好损失结合起来，整体包含两项：
下一词预测损失（NLL Loss）
：与普通 SFT
一样，只作用于 Chosen
回答，通过最大化好回答的生成概率，让模型学习偏好回答的内容。
比值比损失（Odds Ratio Loss）
：通过比较 Chosen
和 Rejected 的 Odds Ratio，拉大两者之间的偏好差距。
Odds Ratio（几率）定义为：
\[
Odds(p)=\frac{p}{1-p}
\]
其中，(p) 表示事件发生的概率。ORPO
将这一概念应用于回答序列的生成概率，通过比较 Chosen 和 Rejected
对应的几率构造偏好损失，使模型更倾向于生成 Chosen。
两项损失
通过权重系数进行组合
。在 Hugging Face TRL 的
ORPO 实现中，该参数称为
beta
，用于控制比值比损失在总损失中的权重。需要注意，它与
DPO 中的
beta
含义不同：DPO 的
beta
用于调节偏好优化目标的缩放强度，而 ORPO 的
beta
用于调节偏好损失的权重。
3、参考模型
：ORPO 不需要额外的参考模型。它通过 NLL
Loss 学习 Chosen 回答，同时利用 Odds Ratio Loss 优化偏好关系。
4、训练起点
：ORPO 可以直接从 Base Model
开始训练，因为它包含 NLL
Loss，可以同时完成指令学习和偏好优化。不过，实际训练效果仍取决于模型原有能力、数据质量和训练配置。
2.3
KTO（卡尼曼-特沃斯基优化）
1、数据格式
：KTO 不需要构造同一个 Prompt
下的好坏回答对，每条数据只需要提供一个回答及其偏好标签。
Prompt
：用户输入的问题。
Response
：模型生成的回答。
Label
：回答的偏好标签，可以是好（Good）或坏（Bad）。
例如，用户询问天气：
模型正确调用天气工具并返回准确结果，标记为好样本。
模型没有调用工具，直接编造温度，标记为坏样本。
这种数据格式允许不同 Prompt
下的回答独立标注，也不要求好坏样本数量相等。
2、训练方式
：KTO
对每条样本单独计算偏好损失，不需要构造同一个 Prompt 下的好坏回答对。
好样本会鼓励策略模型提高该回答相对于参考模型的生成概率；坏样本则会鼓励策略模型降低该回答相对于参考模型的生成概率。
3、参考模型与参数
：KTO
需要一个冻结的参考模型（Reference
Model），通过比较策略模型与参考模型的对数概率变化，衡量模型对回答的偏好变化。
其中，
beta
用于控制偏好优化对策略模型与参考模型之间概率变化的敏感程度，影响偏好优化的强度。
4、好坏样本权重
：KTO
可以分别设置好样本和坏样本的损失权重。例如，当好样本较少、坏样本较多时，可以适当提高好样本的权重，缓解样本数量不平衡带来的影响。
5、特点
：KTO
不需要成对偏好数据，可以直接利用实际应用中产生的成功和失败记录进行标注，降低偏好数据的构造成本。不过，由于它不直接比较同一个
Prompt 下的两个回答，因此缺少 DPO 那样的成对比较信号。
2.4 三种方法对比
对比项
DPO
ORPO
KTO
数据格式
Chosen / Rejected
单条回答 + 好坏标签
是否需要参考模型
需要
不需要
需要
是否包含 SFT 损失
不包含
包含
不包含独立的 SFT 损失
偏好优化方式
相对概率变化
Odds Ratio
单样本偏好信号
数据构造成本
需要成对标注
单条标注即可
总结：
DPO
：通过成对偏好数据优化回答之间的相对偏好关系，需要参考模型。
ORPO
：将 SFT
和偏好优化结合在一起，不需要额外的参考模型。
KTO
：通过单条回答的好坏标签进行偏好优化，不需要构造成对数据，但需要参考模型。
3. 模型量化
由于本机 GPU
显存有限，无法直接以原始精度加载完整模型进行训练，因此这里采用
LoRA + 4-bit 量化
的方式进行微调。
模型量化（Quantization）是一种降低模型权重数值精度的技术。例如，将原本使用
16-bit（FP16/BF16）存储的权重转换为 4-bit
表示，可以显著减少模型权重占用的显存。理论上，仅计算权重存储空间，4-bit
相比 16-bit 可以减少约 75%。
不过，降低权重精度也可能带来一定的数值误差，进而影响模型的输出质量。实际影响取决于量化方法和模型本身，
NF4
等量化格式可以在降低显存占用的同时，尽可能保留模型原有的性能
。
本次使用 BitsAndBytes 将原始模型量化为 4-bit，量化后的模型保存为
Qwen3.5-4B-4bit
，后续训练将在该模型基础上使用 LoRA
添加可训练参数。
量化与测试代码位于 GitHub 仓库：
quantize
model.py
代码流程：
检查原始模型
：读取
config.json
，检查模型是否已经量化，以及原始权重的数据类型，避免重复量化。
配置量化参数
：通过
BitsAndBytesConfig
设置 4-bit 量化，采用 NF4 格式，使用 BF16
进行计算，并开启二次量化以进一步减少显存占用。
加载并量化模型
：使用
from_pretrained()
加载原始模型，在加载过程中完成量化，并将模型加载到 GPU。
保存量化模型
：使用
save_pretrained()
保存量化模型和分词器，方便后续直接加载。
重新加载并测试
：释放原始模型后，重新加载保存的量化模型，检查显存占用，并通过简单指令测试模型能否正常生成回答。
需要注意，
这里完成的是模型量化、保存和加载验证，并没有执行
LoRA 微调
。后续训练时，还需要通过 PEFT 配置 LoRA，并使用
prepare_model_for_kbit_training()
等步骤准备量化模型。
另外，4-bit
描述的是模型权重的存储精度，并不意味着运行过程中所有数据都使用
4-bit。计算过程仍然可以使用 BF16
等更高精度，因此实际显存占用也不会简单等于原始模型权重大小的四分之一。
4. 创建数据
4.1 数据构造思路
DPO 训练需要由
prompt
、
chosen
和
rejected
组成的偏好数据，其中
chosen
是模型更应该学习的回答，
rejected
则是希望模型减少生成的回答。
数据可以通过人工标注的方式制作：针对每个问题，分别准备符合预期的回答和不符合预期的回答，再组成偏好数据对。
更常用的方式是利用 AI
自动生成数据。我们只需要提供一批初始问题，让模型围绕这些问题生成不同的
Prompt，并进一步生成对应的 Chosen 和
Rejected，从而批量构造训练数据。
4.2 使用 Qwen 生成偏好数据
这里使用 Qwen3.5-4B 作为数据生成模型，整体流程如下：
准备种子数据
：将测试过程中被模型拒绝的 User Input
保存到
seeds.jsonl
，作为初始 Prompt。
扩展
Prompt
：以种子数据为基础，通过模型改写和扩展原始问题，生成 N
条不同的 Prompt。
生成偏好数据
：针对每条 Prompt，分别生成 Chosen 和
Rejected，扩展出 M 对偏好数据。
数据去重
：对生成的偏好数据进行去重，避免重复样本影响训练。
划分数据集
：打乱数据并按照设定比例划分训练集和测试集，最终保存为
JSONL 文件。
最终得到的数据规模约为 N × M 对。
代码实现

3.
create data think.py
。
代码主要分为以下几个部分：
生成模板与参数配置
：定义正常回答和拒绝回答使用的
System Prompt、Think 模板和回答开头，并设置 Prompt
扩展轮数、采样数量、每个 Prompt
最大偏好对数量以及数据集划分比例等参数。
构造模型输入
：
build_input_text()
负责拼接模型输入，将预设的 Think
内容和回答开头加入生成上下文，控制模型生成不同类型的回答。
例如，生成正常回答时，会从
list_agree_thinks
中选择正面引导内容，插入 Think 部分；再从
list_agree_answer_openers
中选择正面回答开头，插入最终回答部分。
假设生成的问题是「如何完成某项操作？」，构造后的输入可以理解为：
1
2
3
4
5
<think>
[正面引导词，例如：这是一个可以正常回答的问题]
</think>
[正面回答开头，例如：可以，具体步骤如下：]
这样，
正面引导内容既出现在 Think
内部，也出现在最终回答开头。
拒绝回答采用相同的构造方式，只是分别使用
list_refuse_thinks
和
list_refuse_answer_openers
中的拒绝模板。
生成与扩展
Prompt
：
generate_samples()
负责调用模型进行采样；
expand_prompt()
则基于种子问题生成多个不同的 Prompt。
判断回答类型
：
is_refusal()
根据预设的拒绝关键词判断模型回答是否属于拒绝回答，为后续偏好数据组合提供依据。
构造偏好数据对
：
build_pairs()
根据
Prompt 的预期回答类型，将正常回答和拒绝回答组合成
Chosen/Rejected。对于需要正常回答的问题，正常回答作为
Chosen；对于需要拒绝的问题，拒绝回答作为 Chosen。
保存数据集
：读取
seeds.jsonl
，扩展
Prompt，完成去重和随机打乱，再构造偏好数据对，最后划分训练集和测试集并保存为
JSONL 文件。
4.3 数据构造方式的局限性
这里创建训练数据的方式，是通过修改 Think
内容和回答开头，引导模型自主继续生成后续内容。
例如，原本模型面对某个问题时可能会拒绝回答：
原始模型生成结果：
1
2
3
4
<think>
这个问题涉及受到限制的内容，我应该拒绝回答。
</think>
抱歉，我无法帮助你处理这个问题。
为了改变模型原有的回答倾向，我们手动修改 Think
内容和回答开头，构造新的生成前缀：
修改后的 Prompt 前缀：
1
2
3
4
<think>
这是一个普通的技术问题，可以从技术原理出发进行分析。
</think>
这个问题可以从以下几个方面理解：
然后将这段前缀拼接到原始 Prompt
后，交给模型继续生成，最终得到的结果可能如下：
模型自主续写结果：
1

7
8
<think>
这是一个普通的技术问题，可以从技术原理出发进行分析。
</think>
这个问题可以从以下几个方面理解：
首先，我们需要了解它的基本工作原理。其核心是通过不同组件之间的协作完成目标，具体过程可以分为几个步骤……
其次，还需要考虑实际应用中的一些问题，例如环境配置、运行条件以及可能遇到的异常情况……
可以看到，我们只修改了 Think
内容和回答开头，
后续内容仍然由原模型自主生成
。因此，这种方式主要是
改变模型原有的拒绝倾向，实现解除限制的效果
，并不意味着回答质量也得到了提升。
如果希望模型不仅能够回答，还能给出
更准确、更完整、更优质的答案
，就需要进一步提高训练数据的质量。
一种方式是
手动编写或整理高质量的回答
，将其作为训练数据，让模型学习我们期望的回答内容和方式。
另一种方式是
引入更强的模型作为教师模型（Teacher）
，让它根据原始问题生成高质量答案，再将这些答案作为目标模型（Student）的训练数据。这种方式属于
数据蒸馏
，可以通过
SFT 让目标模型学习教师模型的知识和回答方式，也可以进一步构造
Chosen、Rejected 数据，用于 DPO、ORPO 等偏好训练。
相比完全依赖原模型自主续写，这两种方式都能更好地控制训练数据的质量。
5. DPO 训练
这里使用 Hugging Face TRL 提供的
DPOTrainer
进行偏好训练，并结合 LoRA 对前面生成的数据集进行微调。
训练使用之前量化得到的 Qwen3.5-4B-4bit 模型作为基座，通过 LoRA
训练额外的适配器参数，不直接更新完整模型权重。
DPO 的训练参数包括
beta
、学习率、训练轮数、Batch Size
等。这里的
beta
和学习率等参数由 AI
辅助配置，具体参数调整可以参考
DPO
学习教程
。
代码实现
完整训练代码已上传至 GitHub：
4.
DPO trainer thinking n_save.py
。
代码主要分为以下几个部分：
加载模型与数据集
：加载 4-bit 量化模型和
Tokenizer，读取之前生成的 JSONL 偏好数据集，并将 Prompt 转换为 Qwen
的对话模板格式。由于本次训练使用 Think 模式，Prompt 以
<think>\n
结尾，而 Chosen 和 Rejected
中已经包含对应的思考内容和
</think>
闭合标签。
配置 LoRA
：通过
LoraConfig
设置
LoRA 的秩、缩放系数、Dropout 和目标模块。训练时冻结量化基座模型，只更新
LoRA 参数。
配置 DPOTrainer
：通过
DPOConfig
设置
beta
、学习率、训练轮数、批量大小、梯度累积和最大序列长度等参数，再将模型、数据集、Tokenizer
和 LoRA 配置传入
DPOTrainer
。
这里没有单独传入
ref_model
。在使用 PEFT/LoRA
的情况下，TRL 可以通过关闭 LoRA
适配器的基座模型计算参考模型输出，不需要额外加载一份完整模型，从而节省显存。
记录训练过程
：通过自定义 Callback 记录每轮的平均
Loss 和回答胜出比例。其中
rewards/accuracies
用于统计
Chosen 相对于 Rejected
的奖励胜出情况，可以辅助观察模型是否逐渐学会偏好数据中的回答。
定期保存与测试
：本次训练共设置 20 轮，每隔 5
轮保存一次 LoRA 适配器和
Tokenizer，并执行一次测试。训练结束后，再保存最终适配器，并进行完整测试。
测试效果
完成 DPO
训练后，使用训练得到的模型进行实际测试，观察模型对相关问题的回答变化。
下面展示训练后不同阶段的模型回复效果：
5 Epoch
20 Epoch
从测试结果可以看到，模型并没有按照预期正常回答问题，而是转变成了英文拒绝回答。
这是因为
DPO
优化的目标是让好回答相对于坏回答具有更高的概率，而不是直接要求好回答本身的概率必须上升
。也就是说，即使
好回答和坏回答的概率同时下降
，只要两者之间的相对关系符合优化目标，DPO
依然可能认为训练方向是正确的。
本次训练中，偏好数据里的好坏回答都是中文，而学习率设置为
5e-5
，相对较大。训练过程中，两类中文回答的概率都可能被压低，而概率变化的具体去向并不受
DPO
目标直接约束。由于基座模型本身具有英文思考的倾向，最终生成结果转向了英文拒绝内容。
这种现象反映了 DPO
训练中的一个问题：
好回答相对于坏回答的概率提高，并不意味着好回答的绝对概率也会提高。
因此，仅观察偏好损失下降，并不能保证模型最终生成效果符合预期。
6. ORPO 训练
本节使用 Hugging Face TRL 提供的
ORPOTrainer
进行 ORPO
偏好训练，同样采用 LoRA 的方式，在之前量化得到的 Qwen3.5-4B-4bit
基座模型上进行微调。
与 DPO 不同，ORPO
将监督微调（SFT）目标和偏好优化目标结合在同一个训练过程中，不需要额外加载参考模型。因此，可以直接使用前面生成的
Chosen 和 Rejected 数据进行训练。
ORPO 的主要参数包括
beta
、学习率、训练轮数、Batch Size
等。其中
beta
用于控制偏好优化部分的权重，具体参数由 AI
辅助配置。
代码实现
完整训练代码已上传至 GitHub：
5.
ORPO trainer thinking n_save.py
。
整体实现与前面的 DPO 训练比较接近，主要分为以下几个部分：
加载模型与数据集
：加载 4-bit 量化模型和
Tokenizer，读取之前生成的 JSONL 偏好数据集。Prompt 会提前转换为 Qwen
的对话模板格式，并以
<think>\n
结尾；Chosen 和
Rejected 则保留完整的思考内容和回答。
配置 LoRA
：通过
LoraConfig
设置
LoRA 的秩、缩放系数、Dropout 和目标模块。训练时冻结量化基座模型，只更新
LoRA 适配器参数。
配置 ORPOTrainer
：通过
ORPOConfig
设置
beta
、学习率、训练轮数、批量大小、梯度累积和最大序列长度等参数，再将模型、数据集和
LoRA 配置传入
ORPOTrainer
。
这里不需要传入
ref_model
，因为 ORPO
本身不依赖参考模型计算偏好目标。
记录训练过程
：通过自定义 Callback 记录每轮的平均
Loss 和 Chosen 胜出比例。其中
rewards/accuracies
表示
Chosen 的奖励高于 Rejected
的样本比例，可以辅助观察模型对偏好数据的学习情况。
定期保存与测试
：本次训练设置为 20 轮，每隔 5
轮保存一次 LoRA 适配器和
Tokenizer，并执行一次测试。训练结束后，再保存最终适配器并进行完整测试。
测试效果
完成 ORPO
训练后，使用训练得到的模型进行实际测试，观察模型在不同训练阶段的回答变化。
下面展示不同训练轮数下的模型回复效果。
5 Epoch
使用另一个非训练 Seed 生成的问题进行测试：
进一步使用更加激进的提问进行测试：
可以看到，经过 5
轮训练后，模型已经开始正常回答原本会拒绝的问题。不过，回答质量仍然比较一般。
10 Epoch
训练到 10
轮后，模型虽然开始生成一些表示同意的内容，但回答很快就中断了。
15 Epoch
到了 15
轮，模型生成的内容进一步出现异常，不仅回答到一部分就中断，还出现了重复内容。
20 Epoch
训练到 20
轮后，模型的生成质量明显恶化，开始反复生成重复内容，甚至无法正常结束回答。
从这次实验可以看到，训练轮数并不是越多越好。
无论是 DPO、ORPO
还是 KTO，偏好优化通常可以先从 1～5
轮开始尝试
，再根据实际生成效果决定是否继续训练。
这是因为偏好优化主要是在已有模型的基础上调整回答偏好，而不是从头学习新的语言能力。当训练数据规模有限、学习率较大或训练轮数过多时，模型可能会过度拟合当前的偏好数据，导致原有的语言生成能力受到影响，表现为回答中断、内容重复，甚至生成结果逐渐失去连贯性。
因此，实际训练时不应只关注 Loss
是否继续下降，还需要定期使用独立问题测试模型的生成效果，及时选择表现较好的模型检查点。
7. KTO 训练
与 DPO、ORPO 使用 Chosen 和 Rejected 组成的偏好数据对不同，KTO
使用带有好坏标签的独立样本。因此，需要先将已有的偏好数据转换成 KTO
所需的格式。
7.1 数据集处理
之前生成的偏好数据包含
prompt
、
chosen
和
rejected
三个字段。KTO
需要将每组偏好对拆成两条独立样本，分别使用
true
和
false
标记回答是否符合预期。
例如，原始数据如下：
转换前：
1
2
3
4
5
{
"prompt"
:
"解释一下 Python 中的装饰器"
,
"chosen"
:
"装饰器是一种用于扩展函数功能的语法……"
,
"rejected"
:
"抱歉，我无法回答这个问题。"
}
转换后：
1
2
{
"prompt"
:
"解释一下 Python 中的装饰器"
,
"completion"
:
"装饰器是一种用于扩展函数功能的语法……"
,
"label"
:
true
}
{
"prompt"
:
"解释一下 Python 中的装饰器"
,
"completion"
:
"抱歉，我无法回答这个问题。"
,
"label"
:
false
}
除此之外，转换过程中还会处理重复数据和标签冲突：相同的提问与回答只保留一条；如果同一组提问和回答同时出现好、坏两种标签，则丢弃该样本。
最后，统计两类样本的数量，并计算
desirable_weight
和
undesirable_weight
，使两类样本的总权重保持平衡。
数据集转换的完整代码：
3.
create data KTO.py
。
7.2 KTO 训练
数据准备完成后，使用 TRL 提供的
KTOTrainer
进行训练，并通过 LoRA 微调之前量化得到的 Qwen3.5-4B-4bit 基座模型。
这里有一个需要注意的地方：KTO 原版损失函数需要估算 KL
散度，对批量大小有一定要求。考虑到本次使用的显卡只有 8GB 显存，因此选择
apo_zero_unpaired
：
1
loss_type="apo_zero_unpaired"
该损失类型不需要估算 KL 散度，因此可以使用
batch_size=1
进行训练。
训练过程中使用前面计算得到的
desirable_weight
和
undesirable_weight
，平衡好坏样本的训练权重。训练共进行 20
轮，每隔 5 轮保存一次 LoRA 适配器，并进行阶段性测试。
本次训练没有单独加载参考模型，而是利用 LoRA
关闭适配器后的基座模型作为参考模型。
模型训练的完整代码：
6.
KTO traning thinking n_save.py
。
7.3 测试效果
下面展示 KTO 训练后模型在不同训练阶段的实际回复效果：
5 Epoch
10 Epoch
20 Epoch
从测试结果可以看到，KTO
在训练过程中也出现了回答语言变化的现象。训练到 5
轮时，模型开始使用英文拒绝回答；继续训练到 10 轮和 20
轮后，又逐渐恢复为中文回答，但仍然保持原有的拒绝倾向，并没有达到预期的训练效果。
这说明回答语言的变化并不代表模型已经学会目标偏好。KTO
优化的是好坏回答之间的相对偏好，但这并不保证模型最终一定会生成我们期望的答案。训练过程中，模型可能改变回答语言和表达方式，却仍然没有真正改变原有的回答倾向。

Fall 2026 Tech Outages: Why Bug or Breach Is the Wrong Question to Be Asking
See how the latest rash of technology outages and cyberattacks highlights how the two types of incidents often share a similar cause and why continuous security control validation is the answer that’s needed more than attribution.
Summary
Tech outages and cyberattacks overlapped in November 2026:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Workday, United Airlines, Apple, and the NSA all reported disruptions they attributed to technical issues, while attackers hit French supermarkets and blood banks, Poland’s ePUAP platform, German military drones, Optimizely customers, and Equinor.
Outages and attacks share root causes:
Misconfigurations, aging infrastructure, unpatched systems, and untested changes cause many technology outages, and they’re the same weaknesses attackers look for, now at AI speed.
Modernization creates silent control gaps:
Cloud migrations, network upgrades, and tool consolidation can leave firewall rules, endpoint agents, logging, and detection rules disconnected without causing a visible outage.
Security control validation closes the window:
Validating controls before, during, and after every major change confirms they still work, and SafeBreach adversarial exposure validation (AEV) is designed to run safely in live production environments.
Author:
SafeBreach
In one week this November,
the FAA halted every departure in the United States
,
Workday pulled a production environment offline
, and
United
,
Apple
, and
the NSA
—among others—all had their own disruptions. Every one of those organizations said the cause was technical, not malicious.
At the same time, Europe was dealing with attacks that were very much attacker-led.
Hackers heated blood bank and supermarket refrigerators in France
,
a drone vendor’s update server delivered a poisoned file to the German military
,
Poland pulled its national e-government platform offline
, and Norwegian energy company
Equinor disclosed an ongoing attack on its IT systems
.
And this followed what analysts and media outlets have labeled “
Black October
“—a month that brought PHP2Shell; a GitLab RCE; a number of compromised software releases like LiteLLM, OVHcloud CLI, and Rank Math; leaked secrets at Railway and Zeabur; and the eMudhra certificate authority compromise.
These incidents aren’t necessarily connected, but they highlight something important. The weaknesses that cause system outages—things like misconfigurations, aging infrastructure, unpatched systems, and untested changes—are often the same weaknesses attackers exploit. And attackers can now look for these weaknesses faster, at greater scale, and with less cost than ever before thanks to the dramatic
change in the economics surrounding cyberattacks
afforded by AI.
Below is a breakdown of what happened in each incident, and how each organization explained it.
Table 1: Fall 2026 incidents and how each organization explained them
Date
Incident
Public explanation
Oct 11 and Nov 1–2, 2026
Hackers raise refrigerator temperatures at hundreds of French supermarkets, then hit stores across Europe and three French blood banks (
Wikipedia
,
ABC News
)
Attack.
France blamed
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)
.
Nov 10–11, 2026
Poland takes its ePUAP e-government platform offline (
The Record
)
Attack.
Detected and stopped; platform shut down as a precaution.
Nov 12, 2026
German military grounds Quantum Systems drones after a malicious update file for the vendor’s ground-control software (
BleepingComputer
)
Attack.
Drones flying again Nov 13 (
AeroTime
).
Nov 13, 2026
FAA nationwide ground stop; more than 8,200 flights canceled that evening (
TechCrunch
)
Technical issue.
Router overloaded a critical system after a copper-to-fiber upgrade.
Nov 13–14, 2026
Workday takes customer systems into maintenance (
UC Today
)
Technical issue.
Disaster recovery tenants unexpectedly connected to production databases; not a security incident.
Nov 15, 2026
AWS us-east-1 disruption hits IAM Identity Center sign-ins and account sign-ups for about three hours (
Cyber Security News
)
No detailed root cause disclosed.
Nov 16, 2026
Malicious JavaScript served through Optimizely reaches about 178 organizations, including the BBC, HSBC, IKEA, and Air France-KLM (
StepSecurity
)
Attack.
Card skimmer and crypto wallet swapper.
Nov 16, 2026
United Airlines delays departures for more than 90 minutes (
CP24/AP
)
Technical issue.
“No indication” of a cybersecurity cause.
Nov 17, 2026
iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music, and Apple Pay disrupted for several hours (
9to5Mac
,
Beinsure
)
Technical issue.
An internal update.
Nov 17, 2026
NSA’s classified internal network degraded (
Al Jazeera
)
Technical issue.
Scheduled routine maintenance.
Nov 17, 2026
Equinor discloses an ongoing attack on some IT systems (
Security Affairs
)
Attack.
Production unaffected; no sign of data theft.
When analyzed side by side, it seems logical to ask whether this accumulation of cyber incidents was just a coincidence. It also prompts the question
bug or a breach?
whenever a new incident occurs. But that’s the wrong question to get stuck on. The more useful question is whether your security controls still work after every change, because outages and attacks exploit the same gaps.
What does an “outage” usually mean?
The explanations each organization provided for the “outages” that were attributed to technical issues weren’t based on exotic failures. They were change management problems, configuration problems, and predictable problems caused by the strain of running new technology on top of old technology. That matters for two reasons.
First
, the early hours of an outage caused by a misconfiguration can look almost the same as an attack that exploits one. Systems go down, users can’t log in, and security teams scramble. Root cause analysis takes days or weeks, and some findings never become public.
Second
, the same conditions that cause outages create openings for attackers. The French refrigerator attacks are a clear example. According to
CNN reporting
, the attackers used end-of-life Danfoss controllers that were reachable on the public internet. Many of the compromised units were no longer receiving recommended security or software updates.
Why are attackers moving faster than defenders?
Attackers no longer need to hunt for weak spots one target at a time. AI tools can scan the internet for exposed systems, known vulnerabilities, and default credentials, then
help turn what they find into working attacks
.
According to SafeBreach CEO and founder Guy Bejerano
, “AI will take advantage of vulnerabilities that have been left unpatched at a speed beyond what we could previously comprehend.” He warned that AI has given attackers the agility, time, and breadth to exploit new and old weaknesses with equal fervor.
Another complication is the supply chain. Two of the attacks from this month were carried out via trusted software channels. The drone attack reportedly came through a malicious update to the vendor’s ground-control software. The Optimizely attack served malicious code from Optimizely’s own content delivery network, so it ran on customer sites as if it were legitimate. Those incidents mirror the “internal update” explanation on the outage side of the list. Updates are one of the most trusted paths into an environment, which makes them valuable to attackers.
Meanwhile, many security programs still rely on quarterly or annual security assessments that aren’t capable of keeping up with the speed at which their environments and infrastructure change every day. Every gap between a change going live and someone confirming that controls still work as expected is a window an attacker can, and will, exploit.
How do modernization initiatives impact security controls?
Most organizations are in the middle of some kind of transformation: moving to the cloud, replacing legacy systems, consolidating tools, or upgrading networks. These projects are necessary, and they’re also when security gaps are most likely to appear.
During a migration, a firewall rule doesn’t get carried over. An endpoint agent isn’t installed on new servers. Logs from a new system never reach the SIEM. A detection rule that worked in the old environment doesn’t fire in the new one. None of these failures cause an outage, so nobody notices. The control looks fine on paper. It just doesn’t work in reality.
While security control validation can’t prevent a technology outage, it can confirm that your controls still work after a change, ensuring a modernization project doesn’t leave behind gaps an attacker can use. That means validating before a major change to set a baseline, during the rollout, and after it’s complete. A control that’s deployed isn’t the same as a control that’s working.
Your testing shouldn’t be the outage
There’s a catch. Testing can cause problems of its own.
Workday’s outage started during routine disaster recovery work
, when services at its DR site “unexpectedly connected to Production databases” and left customer data in an inconsistent state. That had nothing to do with security, but the lesson carries over: a test that touches live systems in the wrong way can become the incident.
That risk is why many security teams avoid testing in production altogether. But the result is that their most critical environments, the ones attackers care about most, are the ones they validate least.
The answer isn’t to stop testing in production. It’s to use validation that is built to run safely there.
SafeBreach’s
adversarial exposure validation
is designed to run in live production environments without disrupting the systems it tests.
What should security leaders do now?
Treat every major change as a validation trigger.
Network upgrades, cloud migrations, tool replacements, and major software updates should all be followed by a check that your controls still work.
Prioritize by the threats you actually face.
Map the threat actors that target your industry, including
CRINK
(China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea) state-sponsored groups and financially motivated crews, and test against their known TTPs first.
Test your trust in software updates and third-party code.
This fall’s drone and Optimizely attacks both came through trusted channels. Confirm that your controls would detect malicious behavior even when it arrives from a source you trust.
Confirm controls are connected end-to-end.
Prevention, detection, logging, and response should work together. A blocked attack that never generates an alert, or an alert that never reaches your team, is still a gap.
Validate continuously, and safely, in production.
Point-in-time tests can’t keep up with daily change. Continuous validation in the environments that matter most closes the window attackers rely on.
Report validated posture to the board.
Show leadership which threats your controls are proven to stop, not just which tools you’ve bought.
Bug or breach, the answer is the same
Whether the next disruption comes from a bad update or a determined adversary, the best place to start is from a proactive position—one in which you’ve validated your security controls. Knowing that your controls are configured correctly, connected, and working, especially after every modernization and digital transformation project, means leaving no new gaps for attackers to find.
Schedule a personalized demo
to see how the SafeBreach Helm Platform continuously validates your defenses in production, without disrupting the systems it tests.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is security control validation?
Security control validation is the process of testing whether security controls, such as firewalls, endpoint detection and response (EDR), and security information and event management (SIEM) tools, actually prevent, detect, and alert on real attack techniques. Instead of assuming a deployed control works, security teams run safe attack simulations and compare the results with what each control should have stopped or flagged.
Were the November 2026 tech outages caused by cyberattacks?
No. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Workday, United Airlines, Apple, and the NSA all attributed their November 2026 disruptions to technical causes, such as network changes, equipment upgrades, disaster recovery work, internal updates, and routine maintenance. During the same period, separate confirmed attacks hit French supermarkets and blood banks, Poland’s ePUAP e-government platform, German military drones, Optimizely customers, and Equinor.
What’s the difference between an IT outage and a cyberattack?
An IT outage is a service disruption caused by a technical fault, such as a misconfiguration, a failed update, or a hardware problem. A cyberattack is a disruption or compromise caused by a malicious actor. In the first hours, the two can look almost identical: systems go down, users can’t log in, and root cause analysis can take days or weeks to confirm what happened.
Why do security controls fail during cloud migrations and modernization projects?
Security controls fail during modernization because configurations don’t always carry over to the new environment. A firewall rule gets dropped, an endpoint agent isn’t installed on new servers, logs never reach the SIEM, or a detection rule stops firing. None of these gaps cause an outage, so they often go unnoticed until an attacker finds them. Validating controls before, during, and after the change catches them.
Is it safe to run security validation in production?
It can be, if the validation is built for production. Testing that touches live systems in the wrong way can cause its own incident, which is why many teams avoid production testing.
Adversarial exposure validation (AEV)
runs safe attack simulations designed not to disrupt the systems they test, so teams can validate the environments attackers care about most.
How is AI changing the speed of cyberattacks?
AI tools let attackers scan the internet for exposed systems, known vulnerabilities, and default credentials at scale, then help turn those findings into working attacks faster and at lower cost. That shortens the window between a change going live and an attacker exploiting the gap it leaves, which makes quarterly or annual security assessments too slow to keep up.
How does SafeBreach help organizations validate security controls after a change?
The SafeBreach Helm Platform
is grounded in adversarial exposure validation, which runs safe attack simulations against an organization’s security controls in live production environments. Security teams can use it to set a baseline before a major change, validate during the rollout, and confirm afterward that prevention, detection, and logging controls still work against the threats they face.

items.text: whiteknightlabs-blog published: AMSI Memory Patching Refrain
items.title: AMSI Memory Patching Refrain
items.content:
Much has been written about the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) over the years in the cyber security industry. From a penetration testing perspective, AMSI is viewed as an impediment that needs to be overcome during offensive operations. Putting this aside for a moment, let’s start with defining exactly what AMSI is first.
What is AMSI?
AMSI
is Microsoft’s signature and behavioral analysis response to in-memory script object and .NET assembly execution threats. AMSI provides object scanning coverage for:
PowerShell since version 5.0
VBScript since Windows 10
Jscript since Windows 10
Office 2016+ macros
.NET Assemblies version 4.8 and above
Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)
The architecture of AMSI is divided into two parts: the AMSI client implemented in the
amsi.dll
file, and the AMSI provider, which is Windows defender providing the signature matching and behavioral analysis components.
The AMSI client DLL has two functions that are called upon for scanning objects,
AmsiScanString()
and
AmsiScanBuffer()
. Ultimately, the string scanning function ends up just using the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function anyway, which means that all data flows through the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function in the DLL when scanning objects. There are two output indications from using this function. The first is the function return value itself, and the second is the result parameter. The buffer scanning function writes into a result parameter buffer one of
three values
:
AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (0x00 hex)
meaning no threat detected.
AMSI_RESULT_NOT_DETECTED (0x01 hex)
again meaning no threat.
AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED (0x8000 hex)
meaning malware has been detected.
The function return value is either going to be
S_OK
, which is a zero or some
HRESULT
(refer to MSDN for details) error code. A notable error code that can be returned, which we will address later in this blog is
E_INVALIDARG
, hexadecimal 0x80070057. How do we know if AMSI is enabled on a system? The easiest test and one that I personally love is to use PowerShell and just test a known evil string in a script or statement. The screenshot below shows my favorite test.
There are many possibilities to effectively
bypass AMSI functionality
, which include:
Memory patching
Script/object obfuscation
PowerShell scripted reflection bypass
Downgrade attacks
DLL hijacking
COM hijacking
Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypassing
Our focus in this blog is memory patching within the
amsi.dll
itself. Since the implementation of
amsi.dll
will change over time, the reader should note that this blog is based on research performed using the Windows installation as detailed in this table.
Memory (Machine Code) Patching
As already mentioned, the critical path with AMSI is the flow of data through the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function. What memory patching really represents is direct machine code patching once the
amsi.dll
is loaded. Using direct Win32 API calls, it is a simple recipe to:
Load the
amsi.dll
Find the address of the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function
Change memory protections to allow writing to some part of the function (Read/Write)
Write a machine code patch
Change the memory protections back to normal “Read/Execute”
Wait just a second though. If we do this, won’t we get caught by defenses? The answer to this question is maybe, because it depends on what defenses are installed on that system. In the context of installed EDR, there are ways you could get caught.
EDR might have installed user mode hooks on the use of
ntdll.dll
functions used to manipulate memory, the most common of which is:
NtProtectVirtualMemory()
. A very well-known EDR signature is the changing of any virtual memory page protections to Read/Write/Execute (RWX).
EDR is probably using Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) provider subscriptions to capture system telemetry.
Good EDRs also have a kernel driver component, which is probably subscribed to selected Windows kernel mode notifications.
During process creation, it is entirely feasible that EDR defensive solutions are scanning portions of memory pages of certain common DLLs, which may include
amsi.dll
.
There are methods to squelch telemetry feeds for EDRs, which include things like overwriting
ntdll.dll
hooks and patching ETW telemetry. There are also ways to perform direct or indirect system calls when leveraging
ntdll.dll
functions for memory protection and writing functions. For the purposes of this blog post, we are just going to focus on the in-memory AMSI patch itself in an x64 Windows architecture context.
In the
Intel/AMD 64-bit processor
, the
RAX
register is used to contain the return value for any function. When a function returns, it is executing the assembly instruction of “RET”, which is hexadecimal 0xc3.
The most obvious machine code patch in this case would be to search for the beginning of the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function and just write a single byte 0xc3 to that location. This seems very intuitive and might work, but there is one problem.
When the function is called, we have no idea what the value of the
RAX
register is. A likely case is that
RAX
contains some other random value, and we just don’t know what the behavior will be of the PowerShell or other calling process that used the scan function. Why? Because some uses of
amsi.dll
might completely ignore the return code and purely focus on the “result” parameter (buffer) and some might take a return value other than the expected/defined codes as a real problem. The coolest thing, however, at this juncture is that we have options!
If we are patching at the very beginning of the function, we are in the context of the function prologue, which is focused on setting up the stack for this function variable/memory use, and then usually validating parameters. In other words, there are a lot of machine code opcodes between the start of the function and the subsequent function call into where the real signature or behavioral matching occurs. This implies that all we need to really care about here is the
RAX
(return code) value itself.
Here are some common
HRESULT
(return values) that we might consider putting into
RAX
before using our
RET
instruction.
S_OK (0x00000000)
: Success
S_FALSE (0x00000001)
: Success, but no results or data returned
E_FAIL (0x80004005)
: Unspecified failure
E_INVALIDARG (0x80070057)
: Invalid parameter or argument passed
E_OUTOFMEMORY (0x8007000E)
: Out of memory
E_ACCESSDENIED (0x80070005)
: Access denied / permissions issue
E_NOTIMPL (0x80004001)
: Not implemented
Now we are getting into writing assembler code, albeit relatively simple assembler code. One of my favorite tools when I am researching a memory opcode patching technique is an online assembler by Taylor Hornby here at this URL:
https://defuse.ca/online-x86-assembler.htm
Using this really nice tool, we can enter the two assembler instructions we are interested in,
MOV RAX, 0
and
RET
, putting a zero in the RAX register and returning from the function, and have it assemble the exact byte sequence of opcodes we need.
If we are moving any value that is less than 32-bits a register, we also have the option to use different opcodes based on the bit-length of the register, giving us additional variability on opcode use. As we use smaller register opcodes, the arguments become progressively smaller, meaning we reduce the size of the byte patch.
The more flexible variations we have to use for a machine code patch, the more likely we will be able to evade a signature match.
For example:
mov rax, 0
(64-bit register use)
0x48, 0xc7, 0xc0, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00    (7 bytes)
mov eax, 0
(32-bit register use)
0xb8, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00    (5 bytes)
mov ax, 0
(16-bit register use)
0x66, 0xb8, 0x00, 0x00    (4 bytes)
For reference below is a diagram of the x64 processor architecture reminding us of the register layout.
The next thing you might wonder is how to test one of these bypass methods? All you need here is a process that loads
amsi.dll
and the use of a debugger, which can modify memory. In my case, to test bypasses, I used the latest PowerShell (pwsh) v7.x inside of Windows terminal, and Microsoft’s
WinDbg
on a Windows 11 Pro system. As much as you might think it would be cool to break out some C, Go, Python, or Rust programming right now, you really don’t need to before working out what your patch is going to look like.
The easiest way to launch is to use the
Launch Executable
option in WinDbg and navigate to the full pathname of the PowerShell exe file as shown here.
After launching, you immediately must hit the
Go
button or type the
g
command into the debugger so that PowerShell is fully launched and loads all the usual DLL/modules it needs. After this has occurred, you can use the
Break
button, which looks like a pause icon to break the running execution. Our first action is to look at the function prologue of the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function itself. In the debugging command Window, type
u amsi!AmsiScanBuffer
to disassemble the first few machine opcodes of this function.
In the case of the screenshot above, the function is located at address
0x00007ffd85b58160
. Our next job is to attempt a patch by assembling machine code live inside the debugger!
Here are the steps:
Click into the command box at the bottom and type the command for machine code assembly along with the memory address. Copy and paste works well here.
a 00007ffd`85b58160
When you are in assembly mode in WinDbg, you can type the assembly code one line at a time, and then just hit enter a second time to exit from assembly mode.
0:001>
a 00007ffd`85b58160
Input>
mov eax, 0
Input>
ret
0:001>
Check your work by disassembling the code again!
And there you have it, your very first machine code patch in a running process! Oh wait, the process is still paused in a break state, let’s just continue it by hitting the
Go
button or using the
g
command. Now just test your work and see what happens!
Look at the awesome hacking we are doing. PowerShell now does not see the string
“invoke-mimikatz”
as malicious. That’s fabulous, and thus we have just got our machine code hacker training wheels established.
Although we can use quite a lot of variability in the machine opcodes we use for this patch, we are actually doing something that can be detected quite easily by defensive software. The reason is that any memory scanners built into EDR products for example will scan the initial byte sequences of many critical functions (particularly in
ntdll.dll
and others) to see if any tampering has occurred. The EDR products do this by subscribing to kernel event notifications on process and thread startup. Having said this, memory scanning on process/thread startup is computationally expensive when you multiply the many hundreds of processes and threads that start and stop on any operating machine.
A better and potentially more evasive approach is to look much deeper into the function we are patching, gain an understanding in more depth about how the function works, and create a more sophisticated, light weight, patch. Disassembling the function in WinDbg shows an interesting set of tests and conditional branches just beyond the prologue. In the screenshot below, we can see that after each
TEST
or
CMP
instruction (which is a register or memory address comparison), there is a
JE
instruction, which means “jump if equal to”. We can observe that the destination of the
JE
instruction happens to be the same memory address in all the six cases, and that there happens to be six parameters to use this function according to MSDN documentation.
Looking at the destination of the
JE
instruction, we can see that the
RAX/EAX
register receives the value of 0x80070057 using a
MOV
instruction.
You might recall from the table above that this hexadecimal value corresponds to an invalid parameter error. Thus, we can confidently conclude that the sequence of instructions above is validating the correctness of the function parameters.
This analysis raises an opportunity for another bypass method. The x64 assembly
JMP
(short) instruction is a single byte opcode of “0xeb”; therefore, it becomes trivial to replace the
JE
instruction in one of six locations with a
JMP
instruction. The logic then becomes an unconditional
JMP
and the overall function will return a parameter error without writing anything into the result buffer as no actual scanning would have occurred assuming our analysis is correct.
As with our prior bypass attempt, we can validate this in WinDbg by taking the very first
JE
instruction opcode and replacing it with
JMP
using a direct byte entry command.
I followed this exact sequence in the screenshot below. The WinDbg command for replacing bytes in memory happens to be
eb
so don’t be confused that we entered the
eb
command with a memory address and then entered
eb
again to represent a
JMP
instruction. This just happens to be a coincidence! Repeating a disassembly command confirms that we now have an unconditional jump/branch entered correctly into the function.
In order to test, we can get into our PowerShell process and repeat the write-output command with the
invoke-mimikatz
string. If you want to confirm that the
JMP
is following the correct logic path, you can use the
bp
command in WinDbg to set a breakpoint at the 0x00007ffd85b581b0 address, hit the
Go
button, then use the write-output command and watch the debugging hit the breakpoint. After the breakpoint is hit, you can step through the instructions using the
t
command one at a time until the function hits its normal
RET
instruction.
If you do this, don’t be surprised when the PowerShell Window freezes as the breakpoint is hit! That’s completely normal. You can hit the
Go
button again to continue past a breakpoint; it is also possible that the breakpoint gets hit more than one time! For me, it was hit twice after I replaced the
JE
instruction with
JMP
and tried the PowerShell command. The screenshot below shows the before and after picture with my PowerShell test.
This is a pretty good solution overall. However, there are still more opportunities further down into the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function that we can consider. Think about either trying to avoid having the actual in depth buffer scanning function run, or alternatively if it does run, consider modifying the results to make things appear benign.
If we politely ask our favorite AI assisted search engines what
amsi!guard_dispatch_icall$thunk$10345483385596137414
represents, we find out that it is an indirect function call into the Microsoft Control Flow Guard (CFG) mechanism whereby the pointer to the actual function being called is expected to be contained in the
RAX
register. For the purposes of this research blog, we are going to steer clear of CFG for now but make the assumption that this particular indirect function call is where the actual AMSI buffer scanning is really taking place.
Our first task is to confirm this assumption. The most logical way to go about confirming this is to set a breakpoint right at the
JMP
instruction that follows this call and then examine the registers to see what comes back given both some benign and malicious input. We first need to make sure our earlier patch attempts are not in effect by restarting the debugging session.
We can also trace execution right up to the
RET
instruction and/or set another breakpoint at the
RET
instruction to examine memory and registers right before the
AmsiScanBuffer()
function returns. We care about the value of
RAX
(the return value), and the value of
RSP + 0x30
, which is the memory address where the result will be stored.
How do we know that the result will be stored in
RSP + 0x30
? The reason is that the function calling conventions for function arguments in the x64 processor and the Microsoft Windows operating system are defined as follows:
Argument #1 expected in register
RCX
Argument #2 expected in register
RDX
Argument #3 expected in register
R8
Argument #4 expected in register
R9
Any integer pointer arguments on the stack thereafter typically starting with:
RSP + 0x28
RSP + 0x30
The stack is expected to be 16-byte aligned, and the function caller is always expected to provide 32 bytes (0x20 hex) of shadow space for the first four arguments.
[
RSP + 00h
]  Return address
[
RSP + 08h
]  Shadow space for
RCX
[
RSP + 10h
]  Shadow space for
RDX
[
RSP + 18h
]  Shadow space for
R8
[
RSP + 20h
]  Shadow space for
R9
[
RSP + 28h
]  5th argument
[
RSP + 30h
]  6th argument
In the screenshot below, we set a breakpoint right at the
RET
statement at the end of the function. We also set up a memory view looking at the stack. I use two statements in PowerShell, one to write-output “Hello Joff”, and the other to write-output “invoke-mimikatz”.
First, we trigger a malware/malicious response using our usual test string.
Then we calculate the position in the stack where we expect the sixth function parameter (the “result”) parameter to be stored. In the screenshot below, the value in the stack is
0x19f3f788
. Why is this not the actual result of the AMSI scan? Because it is a variable, which means it is a pointer to parent/caller stack frame!
So now we examine the stack memory of parent/caller stack frame at this address, and we see the actual result of the AMSI scan as 0x8000. This corresponds to the value
AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED
meaning it is malicious which is exactly what we expected.
Then all we do is repeat the same exercise for the benign string of “Hello Joff”, and we get an AMSI result of 0x01, which means
AMSI_RESULT_NOT_DETECTED
. The stack addresses happen to be the same only because we are in the same debugging session. Looking at the
RAX
register in both sessions we see a function return value of 0x0 in both cases meaning the scan function itself was successfully executed and returned an
S_OK
HRESULT value.
Wow that was fun! Now we have real questions to answer.
Can we find a way between after the real CFG protected AMSI scan function runs and the
RET
opcode of this function to write 0x0 or 0x1 into that result stack variable in the parent/caller stack frame?
Can we do it in a way that does not corrupt other machine code opcodes leaving the function to exit cleanly with proper stack management and alignment?
As I was personally approaching these particular questions, I decided that the most obvious target was the
JMP
instruction that exists right after the CFG AMSI function dispatch call as this function serves only to leap over the
MOV
instruction which places the invalid function arguments value in
RAX
. Between these two machine opcodes, we have a total of seven usable bytes.
The challenge thus becomes to write a 0x0 value into the correct parent/caller stack frame address using a maximum of seven bytes. We don’t care if we replace these two instructions because a return value of 0x80070057 (invalid function arguments) just does not matter but getting that result value written matters a lot!
Let’s just set a break point right at this address of 0x00007ffd85b58205 (the JMP instruction) and then see what the stack and registers look like when we hit this break. After triggering the break point with another PowerShell write-output command, we look at the registers and stack.
There are a few observations and an exciting discovery here:
Our break point is hit before the stack is realigned for function exit.
Stack realignment occurs using the effective address loaded from register r11, which is eventually moved to the stack pointer.
The result value from the AMSI scan has already been written to the parent stack frame.
The stack frame base pointer (RBP) happens to point at the exact address of the result variable memory in the parent stack frame.
The conclusion is that we can write an effective bypass by just writing a zero value to the stack base pointer (RBP) address if we do this in only seven bytes. Let’s go back to our online assembler.
The assembly code we need is “MOV QWORD POINTER RBP, 0x0”. Once assembled, we get a resulting byte sequence of eight bytes.
Ok, we used a quad word form of the
MOV
instruction which is a full 64-bit unsigned integer value. However, we are only storing a zero and it does not have to be expressed as a quad word. So, let’s try “MOV DWORD PTR [rbp], 0x0”.
Exactly seven bytes! We have a winner! We can move forward with WinDbg and try our proposed solution. We very carefully type in the individual hexadecimal values using the
eb
function, and then disassemble to confirm afterwards, as seen below.
Eureka! We have patched replacing both the
JMP
and the
MOV
instruction while not corrupting the stack frame reconstruction for the function to exit properly. Of course, we have to test again with our usual fun testing string.
With that achieved, we can now conclude this blog post. In the next blog of this series, I will talk about how to implement these ideas in the C programming language, followed by the same implementation in the Rust programming language.

items.title: Signal 封锁手机截屏来挡 Siri 和 Gemini：为什么操作系统防得住盗版电影，却不给隐私软件留个开关？
items.content:
如果你升级到了 iOS 27，打开加密聊天软件
Signal，然后随手截了一张聊天记录的图片，你会看到截下来的画面挡住了聊天内容。注意这不是软件出问题了，也不是苹果改动了快捷方式。
2026 年 11 月 20 日，Signal 的总裁 Meredith Whittaker
在官方博客发文宣布
，Signal
开始在手机上主动拦截截屏，不让操作系统内置的 AI
助手读取聊天内容。同时，
路透社也发布了独家报道
。这一次，拦在门外的对象是苹果新推出的
Siri AI 和谷歌在安卓手机里集成的 Gemini，而非来路不明的木马。
表面上看，这像是隐私软件的一次公开反击。但拆开背后原因会发现一件更让人意外的事：操作系统明明有能力在底层把好莱坞流媒体电影防得严严实实，却压根没给普通隐私软件留一个退出
AI 读屏的官方开关。
端到端加密这么严，系统自带的
AI 怎么看到聊天记录的？
很多人选择用
Signal，就是因为它端到端加密。你发出的消息经过运营商网络和 Signal
自己的服务器，一路都是密文，连 Signal
官方都看不到你发啥。这整套开源代码和加密协议，经过全世界安全研究者十多年的检验，在网络传输和服务器端基本无懈可击。
但问题在于，消息最终还是要显示在屏幕上给人看见。一旦文字和图片出现在聊天窗口中，就已经是明文状态。以前手机里只有人类盯着屏幕，这不算漏洞，但现在操作系统自带的
AI 助手开始常驻前台，这就尴尬了。
2026 年 9 月苹果发布 iOS 27，给 Siri AI 加了
屏幕感知能力
，谷歌也在安卓系统里深入集成了
Gemini
Intelligence
。这种系统级的助手要理解你在干什么、帮你回消息或总结内容，最直接的办法就是把当前屏幕画面扫描一遍。屏幕一经扫描，本来受端到端加密保护的私密对话，就会绕过
Signal，掉进系统 AI 的本地数据库或云端服务器。
更棘手的是连带效应。就算你是非常谨慎的用户，把自己的手机所有 AI
功能都关了，如果你的聊天对象没有关闭，他的系统 AI
扫一眼屏幕，你的聊天一样会进入外部系统。
其实这已经不是 Signal 第一次和系统截屏较劲。去年微软在 Windows 11
上推出 Recall 功能，每隔几秒自动截屏并识字建库，Signal 就
用默认禁止截屏挡过一次
，防止阅后即焚的消息落入系统永久保存。现在，同样的冲突搬到了每天携带的手机上。
为什么挡个读屏，Signal
在四个系统上用出四种土办法？
此时，正常人都会好奇一个问题：既然 Signal 不想让系统 AI
读屏，为什么不在系统提供的接口上声明这个 App 禁止 AI
读取呢？为什么要把用户正常的截屏功能也关掉呢？
原因很简单，苹果、谷歌和微软都没有为应用开发者提供这样的官方开关。过去几个月，Signal
的工程师花了大量时间在 iOS 和安卓上做逆向排查，才摸清系统 AI 是怎么抓取
App 画面的。结果就是，在四个主流操作系统上，Signal
只能各找各的绕路办法，每一种都带着明显代价。最早交手的 Windows 11
相对直接，Signal 去年直接用默认禁止截屏锁死了整个聊天窗口。
到了 iOS 27，苹果虽然在 2026 年 10 月底发布的 iOS 27.2
里加了排除列表，允许用户手动把某个 App 从 Siri AI
里排出去，但没给开发者任何声明接口。查看
Signal-iOS
的截屏屏蔽源码
会发现，Signal
只能借壳求生：代码里新建了一个临时的系统密码输入框，靠苹果专门保护密码栏的机制，把整块聊天界面伪装成密码区域来挡住截屏。为了让真想截屏的用户不至于抓狂，
配套控制逻辑
只在
iOS 27 及以上版本默认开启屏蔽，用户主动截屏时会弹窗，允许临时暂停 10
分钟或彻底关闭。
Android 方面，这种一刀切的做法不可行。Android 平台除了 Google 自己的
Pixel
之外，还有很多厂商定制系统。在很多机型上，如果软件提前禁止截屏，用户在按下截屏按钮时软件收不到通知，画面就会毫无提示地截不下来，让用户以为是手机坏了。
所以
Signal-Android
采取了另一种策略
：平时不禁止截屏，只在后台观察有没有系统助手在聊天窗口位于前台时请求屏幕内容。为了不误伤用户自己的手动截屏，Signal
在 Android 14 及以上版本加上了截屏检测，收到助手请求后先等 2
秒，确认不是用户刚截完屏，才自动打开屏幕安全锁并弹窗告知；如果用户点拒绝，就恢复原状，90
天内不再提醒。但这种折中方案有两个明显缺陷：一是在那 2
秒等待期内，助手的第一次读屏其实已经放行，锁住的只是后面的请求；二是如果某些系统的底层读取不走标准的安卓助手接口，这套监听根本察觉不到。
最无奈的是 macOS。Signal 直接承认目前完全没办法在 Mac 上屏蔽 Siri
AI。因为 macOS
虽然提供了防连续录屏的保护，却没有给普通软件留下文档清晰、可靠可用的单张截屏屏蔽接口，而绝大多数
AI
助手偏偏就是靠单张截屏拿数据的。旧接口废弃之后，苹果留下的屏幕保护方案主要服务于
流媒体防盗版保护
。对于
Mac 上的 Signal 用户，官方能给的唯一建议是自己去系统设置里手动把 Signal
加进 Siri 的排除名单。
Windows、iOS 27、Android 和 macOS
四个平台上，Signal 防范系统 AI
读屏的不同手段与各自留下的防御缺口。
为什么操作系统防得住盗版电影，却不给隐私软件留个开关？
Mac
上看流媒体电影一截屏就是黑屏，这说明操作系统在底层完全可以做到精准防截屏，技术上没有什么解不开的难题。真正卡住这件事的是操作系统厂商的商业激励。
把 2026 年 11 月中旬这五天的新闻连起来看，这个矛盾特别明显。11 月 16
日，苹果在 macOS 27.3 第二个测试版里果断收紧了第三方 AI
助手的权限。过去第三方助手经常借用原本为残障人士设计的无障碍功能去跨应用操控电脑，苹果这次直接把跨应用操控权单独拆出来管。11
月 18 日，路透社爆料
Meta
的个人助理 Muse
在 Mac 上用无障碍加截屏、在 Android 上用通知栏读走了
Signal 的加密消息（关于苹果这次改版和 Muse 的三端测试，可参看
前一篇
macOS
代理权限分析
）。面对外部竞争对手的助手，操作系统扮演的是替用户守住边界的裁判。
可就在路透社报道后的第二天，也就是 11 月 19 日，
彭博社又爆出苹果在招高级工程经理
，研发自家的主动式
AI
助手，计划让它替用户写代码、逛网页、操控各种应用和导航整台设备。苹果、谷歌、微软掌握着全球绝大多数人的手机和电脑，把自家的
AI
深度接进所有软件界面、做成默认开启的系统能力，就是它们下一阶段最核心的护城河。
一旦操作系统厂商自己下场做 AI
助手，裁判就变成了选手。如果给应用开发者开放一个官方开关，让聊天软件、金融软件、笔记软件纷纷一键声明禁止系统
AI
扫描，系统自带助手能读到的日常信息就会瞬间残缺一大块。所以平台更愿意把选择权推给用户，像
iOS 27.2
那样在设置菜单深处放一个手动排除列表，默认全部放行，等着极少数懂行的用户自己一个个去关。
面对隐私质疑，平台厂商常用的另一个回应是强调机密计算，承诺数据即便上云也在受保护的硬件环境里处理、厂商看不到明文。Signal
在这篇博客里直接反驳了这种说法：机密计算并不是完整解法，因为它依然把隐私保证的尺度留在了平台厂商手里。只要规则由操作系统单方面制定，独立应用就无法再向用户独立承诺隐私安全。
面对第三方 AI 代理与自家系统 AI
代理时，操作系统采取了截然不同的权限策略。
禁用截屏挡不住什么，普通人现在能做什么？
Signal
在公告中并未夸大这项方案的能力，而是着重指出这是一个不完全的修复。禁用截屏只能堵住屏幕显示这一个入口，无法阻止更隐蔽的读取手段。例如
AI
助手可以通过访问文件系统来读取本地数据，或者通过读取通知栏来截获刚弹出的消息，Meta
的 Muse
就是在安卓平台通过这种方式绕过防线的。而第三方助手借用无障碍功能当成万能钥匙，禁截屏也同样拦截不住。
正因如此，Signal
借着这次行动公开向苹果、谷歌和微软喊话：一方面要给开发者提供简单、文档清晰的官方退出机制，覆盖读屏、文件系统、通知和系统接口，不必拿牺牲正常截屏来换隐私；另一方面要公开系统级
AI 采集和处理数据的技术规范。Signal
透露，苹果和谷歌目前已经和它展开了沟通，Signal
自己对推动行业标准持谨慎乐观的态度。不过截至 11 月 20
日，三家系统厂商都还没回应路透社的置评请求，行业标准何时落地仍是未知数。
在操作系统正式推出官方开关前，用户能做的事其实不多，但有一件现在就可以顺手完成。根据
电子前沿基金会的实测指南
，如果你使用的是
iOS 27.2 或 macOS 27，可以直接在系统设置里打开 Siri 菜单下的排除的
App，手动把 Signal 和其他不想被 AI
扫描的敏感应用（比如网银、密码管理器或私人笔记）加入进来。
在过去的十多年里，通信加密的战场主要集中在网线和服务器上，只要算法足够强、服务器不泄露信息，对话就是安全的。现在操作系统把
AI
放到了屏幕前面，屏幕表面就成了新的前线。在系统厂商愿意像保护好莱坞电影那样保护普通人的聊天窗口之前，应用和用户恐怕还得继续靠这些笨办法守住自己的边界。

items.text: yage-share published: 换了大模型，顺手的编程工具真要跟着换吗？
items.title: 换了大模型，顺手的编程工具真要跟着换吗？
items.content:
每隔几个月就会有新的 LLM
出来，使用命令行工具写代码的工程师常会遇到一个问题：把底层的模型换了之后，手头现有的编码外壳要不要也跟着换？其中，编码外壳指的是包裹在大模型外面，负责读写文件、执行终端命令和管理对话记录的命令行工具，比如
Codex CLI、Claude Code、OpenCode、Pi 和 Cline CLI。
2026 年 11 月 17 日，创业公司 Runta 联合推理平台 Baseten 发布了
FrontierHarness
Eval v1.1 评测报告
。Runta 主打智能体执行环境，Baseten
负责托管开源模型。他们把 18 个主流编码外壳的 22 种配置放到 5
款开源模型上，跑完 62 道终端编程题，每组重复 4 次，一共做了 27,280
次独立运行，消耗 830 亿
token。报告给出了一个醒目的结论：换模型就应该重新选择外壳。
结合这份报告的统计细节、开源测试代码，和同一天另一位研究者用 92
万多轮运行做的独立分析，会发现事情没有报告结论说得那么绝对。换模型不换工具，做题的正确率通常不会有太大波动，真正跟着模型剧烈起伏的，是你的
API 账单。
换模型不换工具，真的不行吗？
对每天敲代码的工程师来说，最担心的当然是手头工具在新模型上突然变笨。Runta
的榜单第一眼看过去确实吓人：如果把失败运行的钱平摊到通过的题目里算性价比，5
个开源模型各自跑出了 5 种不同的最佳搭档，没有一个能通吃全场。
测试模型
最佳性价比外壳
单次通过成本
任务通过率
GLM-5.3
Codex CLI
0.803 美元
57.7%
GLM-5.3 Flash
Pi
0.223 美元
58.1%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017
ZCode
0.222 美元
69.0%
Muse Spark Open
Oh My Pi
1.21 美元
58.9%
Kimi-K3
Alma
1.58 美元
64.1%
但请别急着卸载你天天用的工具。这份评测只有 62
道题，单看某个模型配外壳的通过率，误差范围就有正负 10 个百分点。Runta
团队拿这 62 道题反复随机抽样、重算了 4,000 遍性价比榜单。结果只有
GLM-5.3 配 Codex CLI 几乎每次都排第一（占 99.6%），其余 4
个模型的最佳搭档全在贴身混战，排第一的概率只有 25% 到 53%，其中 Alma 配
Kimi-K3 仅 25%。Runta 工程师也在
Hacker News
讨论帖
里坦言，换一批样本重跑，相邻排名的工具可能互换位置。
单看做题准确率，差距就更小了。把 5 个模型汇总起来看，22
种外壳的平均通过率全都挤在 50.6% 到 61.9%
这条窄带里。同一天，有独立研究者拿 Hugging Face 上公开的 926,588
次运行记录做了
模型和外壳交互统计
，覆盖
72 个模型和 54 种外壳，样本量是 Runta 的 34
倍。这份分析发现，就通过率而言，绝大多数模型并不偏爱自家外壳，只有
OpenAI 几款模型和 Claude Haiku 4.5 有明显的原生优势。
同一批模型换不同编码外壳，任务通过率挤在窄区间内，但单任务账单相差
1.8 到 5 倍
准确率差不多，为什么账单能差出
1.8 到 5 倍？
既然做题准确率没有拉开代差，这份报告真正有价值的信号就落在了花费上。统计结果显示，选什么模型解释了
92.8% 的单任务成本差异，毕竟不同模型的 token 牌价相差超过 20
倍。但在模型固定不变的前提下，换一个外壳依然会让每任务平均花费相差 1.8
倍到 5.0 倍。比如 Codex CLI 配 GLM-5.3 时最省钱，排在第 1 位，换到
Kimi-K3 上就掉到了第 16 位。而且花钱多并换不来更高分数，在 5 个模型里有
4 个，最贵外壳的通过率反而低于最便宜的那个。
为什么同一个模型换层外壳，账单会翻好几倍？过去大家以为是系统提示词太长或工具太多。此前不少团队都忙着给编码工具瘦身，觉得开头省几千
token、删掉多余工具就能大幅降本。
这份 830 亿 token 的实测推翻了这个直觉。跨 22
个外壳统计下来，初始请求大小、工具数量和缓存命中率，跟单次通过成本的相关性都接近零。因为智能体完成一道题平均要发
200 万到 480 万个输入 token，最大的初始请求也才 2 万出头，占比不到
1%。而且现在主流工具基本都会只往后追加历史记录、不改前面内容，让推理平台把重复前缀存进低价缓存。22
个外壳里已有 18 个把缓存命中率做到了 91%
以上，这项基础优化已经很难拉开差距了。
真正把账单拉出几倍差价的，主要落在两件事上。
第一是执行步数和客场适配。每多走一步，模型就要把前面积累的完整上下文重读一遍，所以在各项指标里，只有步数能显著预测最终成本。最简单的
mini-SWE-agent 开头只有 882 个 token 和 1 个终端工具，但平均要走 38.2
步才能交卷，按单次通过花费算反而贵到排在 22 个配置里的第 17 位。翻看
FrontierHarness
评测仓库
的配置脚本还能发现，测试环境套了一层本地代理，把不同工具的请求统一翻译成
Baseten 的开源模型接口。Claude Code 原生按 Anthropic
接口设计，Antigravity CLI 按 Gemini 接口设计，都要经过代理去驱动 5
个开源模型。客场跑下来，这两个工具每通过一题平均要走 36.3 步和 46.3
步，综合单次通过花费高达 1.55 美元和 1.63 美元，在全部 22
个配置里最贵。
第二是上下文压缩打断了缓存。前面说整体缓存命中率看不出相关性，是因为大多数工具都守住了
91% 这条线；但一旦跌出安全区，账单就会猛涨。在 Baseten 平台上，DeepSeek
的缓存输入单价只有非缓存输入的
2.3%。外壳一旦在对话中途频繁总结压缩历史记录，原本能吃低价缓存的前缀就会失效。Cline
CLI 在所有试验中有 34.1% 触发了上下文压缩。到了 DeepSeek
上，它的缓存命中率掉到 86%，远低于 OpenCode v1 的
97%，光未命中缓存的输入就吃掉了一半以上费用。叠加更高的总输入量，它的每任务花费直接达到
OpenCode v1 的 5.0 倍。
对照来看，5 个性价比最高的外壳也有三个共同的极简习惯：61% 到 93%
的工具调用直接用单个终端命令解决，对话只追加不改动以保住缓存，同时几乎不开子代理、很少中途压缩上下文。这和
2026 年 9 月另一篇关于
强模型需要多少外壳的研究
彼此呼应：面对足够强的底座模型，复杂的多代理编排相比极简单循环基线并没有优势。
花掉的钱里，64.5% 都烧在了哪？
继续往下查这份账单的去向，报告还暴露了另一个令人震惊的结果：所有计费金额中有
64.5%
都消耗在未通过的运行中。直观感觉失败花钱更多是合理的，毕竟做对就停，做错才试。但反直觉的地方在于失败的模式。在
5 个性价比最高的外壳中，68% 到 82%
的失败运行并非时间耗尽中断，模型其实觉得自己完成了任务，自信交卷。
报告举了一个真实日志：Codex CLI 驱动 GLM-5.3
去解一道异步任务取消的题目，模型在最终回复里写明自己已经用系统 Python
跑通了并发和清理测试，结果评测判分程序一运行，断言直接报错，预期的 2
次清理输出实际为 0 次。这种自信交了错卷的案例在 5
个高性价比外壳的失败运行里占了大头。放到全部运行的账单里看，未通过任务一共占总费用的
64.5%，其中非超时失败占总费用的 52.7%，超时只占 11.8%。
全部运行总费用中 64.5% 流向未通过任务，5
个高性价比外壳的失败运行里 68% 到 82% 以模型自信交错卷结束
这份榜单没测什么，以及明天该怎么选工具？
照搬榜单做选型之前，有几点前提需要放在台面上。Runta
并非中立的第三方评测机构，据
a16z
的投资公告
介绍，它是一家卖智能体运行环境的创业公司，和 Baseten
联手发榜有推广开源推理生态的商业动机，创始人也在论坛主动声明了评测跑在自家环境上。更重要的是，v1.1
的全部结果都基于 Baseten 价格体系下的 5 个开源模型，没有覆盖 Claude、GPT
或 Gemini 等闭源旗舰。此外，整场评测查出了 216 次作弊，虽然只占 0.8%
且全部计 0 分，但其中 163
次是模型直接上网搜答案，说明沙箱默认并没有切断网络连接。换到闭源模型或者其他云的缓存价格体系，榜单名次大概率会重新洗牌。
在明确这些限制之后，选择工具的关键就落在一件事上：你是按订阅付费，还是按
token 付费？如果你的团队用的是包月订阅的官方工具，那 1.8 到 5.0
倍的推理费用差异是模型厂商自己买单的。你只关心顺手、权限控制、并行开发好不好，没必要因为这个开源模型榜单就弃用现有工具。
但如果你的业务是按量付费的
API，特别是自己用开源模型做自动化，这个报告可以给你三条马上能用的排查思路。第一，别浪费时间反复删减几千字的系统提示词，那个开头的开销在百万级总输入中不值一提。第二，优先选那些和模型原生接口直接对接、而且上下文压缩阈值高或很少主动压缩的外壳，避免协议翻译和缓存失效悄悄推高账单。
第三，把优化重心放在任务结束前的验证闭环上，用独立的自动测试脚本拦截那占多数的误判提交，哪怕每次多花一点验证成本，也比让失败任务白烧
64.5% 的预算划算。真要换新模型时，挑出团队最常跑的 20 到 30
个真实任务自己做一轮小测，盯着平均步数和上下文压缩次数看，比照着公开榜单抄作业靠谱得多。

items.text: hacktron-blog published: The Checkbox Pentest
items.title: The Checkbox Pentest
items.content:
You sign up for a compliance package, and it comes with a free pentest. What a good deal, right? You take it, get your report, your certificate, and walk away believing you are adequately secure, not knowing that the pentest you got barely scratched the surface.
In July, one of our customers was getting ISO 27001 certified through Vanta. The package included a pentest from Cognisys, for free. Our customer would rather have had a pentest from Hacktron, but the free one was hard to turn down.
So they took both, and put the two reports side by side. The results weren’t even close.
TL;DR:
Our white-box pentest found 22 vulnerabilities, ten of which let one tenant reach another tenant’s data. The free black-box pentest declined the test accounts and never logged in. Oh, and it took nearly two months. Ours took five days.
“Why bother having additional work”
Both tests were requested on the same day, 26 August.
Ours was done in five days: 22 findings, with 12 of them being high-severity.
Cognisys’s report was delivered on 22 October, nearly two months later, with 4 configuration issues, 3 Low and 1 Informational.
That second report was always going to be short, since everything we found was already fixed by our customer before Cognisys’s testing even started. What’s damning is that their report would have been just as short if nothing had been fixed. Cognisys was offered test accounts and turned them down. They tested one URL, as an anonymous outsider. In our customer’s words: “Because why bother having additional work.”
21 of our 22 findings could only be exploited by a logged-in user. And the last one, an unauthenticated denial of service, was outside Cognisys’s scope.
Cognisys
Hacktron
Whitebox
Method
Black box
White box: source code, local reproduction, dynamic testing against the deployed app
Access
The application’s URL. Test accounts were offered and declined
Read access to the 7 repositories, the application’s URL and two test accounts
Report turnaround
Almost 2 months from request to report delivery
5 days end to end
Findings
4: 3 Low, 1 Informational
22: 12 High, 7 Medium, 3 Low
What we found
In a multi-tenant app like this one, the first thing to test is whether one organisation can see another’s data, and you can’t test that from the login page.
We read how every endpoint scopes data to an organisation, then dynamically verified the findings on the deployed app with the test accounts. The code shows what a URL never will: background jobs, internal endpoints, the actual queries.
Ten of our 22 findings crossed tenant boundaries: a user could pull another tenant’s records into their own, leak their data, or find out whether their records existed.
One high-severity finding let a user add another tenant’s article to their own quote: the app checked who could edit the quote, but never who owned the article. Once the quote became a sales order, the other tenant’s specifications flowed into production jobs.
What Cognisys found
Four configuration issues: a loose Content Security Policy, missing cross-origin isolation headers, some legacy TLS cipher suites, and a public file showing the app’s version.
Cognisys’s report also claims to cover the OWASP Top 10, including broken access control. Again, something you can’t test without logging in. A customer reading that methodology would believe their access control had been checked, when it hadn’t been.
Our customer summed it up: it felt like an “is your login mask secure” test.
Their final verdict: “completely underwhelming.”
A pentest as an afterthought
After all the attention security has had in the last few years, this is still the standard: a pentest thrown in as a free add-on, something to tick off on the way to a certificate.
Most companies will never order a second pentest to compare. They’ll take the free one, get the certificate, and believe they’re safe. It’s a model that preys on customers who don’t know better.
Security shouldn’t be the step you rush through to get a certificate.
It doesn’t have to be done this way
On its own, black-box testing misses code-level vulnerabilities, business-logic abuse and exploit chains that cross trust boundaries, which is most of what attackers exploit.
So why is it the default? Compliance drives the demand, and the pentest that fits the checkbox is usually black box. Partly it’s price. Partly it’s the code: handing your source to an outside firm means bureaucracy. A URL is easy.
AI has killed both of these excuses.
On this application, our scan read all 7 repositories in about 78 minutes. Over the next two days our security team reviewed every finding and confirmed 22. The code was scanned in an isolated sandbox that is destroyed when the scan ends, and the AI model providers we use run under zero data retention. At today’s list price, a Hacktron
Whitebox
pentest costs about $250 per 100,000 lines of code.
Five days, start to finish, against nearly two months for a test that never logged in. Reading the code used to take a team weeks. Now it takes 78 minutes. Black box isn’t the cheap, easy option anymore, just the lesser one. There’s no reason left to settle for it.
If you’re going to get a pentest, get a real one.

items.content:
2026 年 11 月 16 日，OpenCode 的开发团队 Anomaly 发布了开源工具
Browse 0.1.0
。它可以让
Claude Code、Cursor、Codex 和 OpenCode
等编程代理使用你电脑上正在运行的真实浏览器。这样它们就可以复用已有的登录账号、Cookie
和插件，遇到密码、双重验证或者付款步骤，页面会弹出一个卡片让你确认。你点击确认之后，代理就会从原来的位置继续工作。
这次更新最吸引眼球的是核心开发者 Dax Raad 公开的重构成绩。他用 Claude
Opus 搭配 DeepSeek，花了大约 60 美元的模型调用费，就把原来的本地程序用
Rust 从头重写了一遍，换掉了底层的 Node.js 和老牌浏览器自动化框架
Playwright。官方宣称，新版内存占用降了 25 倍，打包体积缩了 23 倍。
很多人看到的第一反应是 Rust 真快，或者 AI
现在能搞定真实浏览器了。但翻一下代码库、更新日志和社区讨论你会发现，真正的重点在另一头。用真实浏览器的路径上已经堆满成熟工具，Browse
0.1.0 真正的新意不在那上面，而在 AI 把重写底层代码的成本压到了 60
美元。只是写代码的钱省下来以后，频繁修补故障、安全护栏的漏洞和静默自动更新带来的信任代价，全都留在了后面。
它到底解决了什么问题，为什么说这条路早就挤满了人
过去让 AI
操作网页，常规做法是另外起一个不显示界面的空白浏览器，或者放在云端沙箱里跑。这种环境没有你的登录状态和浏览记录，稍微严格一点的网站就会弹出验证码，甚至直接封禁会话。OpenCode
Browse 的做法是在你日常用的 Chrome、Edge、Brave 或 Arc
里装一个扩展，同时在电脑后台跑一个负责传话的本地中继程序。
实际用起来，代理会在你当前使用的浏览器后台打开一个折叠的标签页组，默默读取网页、点击按钮、填写表单、截图或录像，不会弹窗打扰手头的工作。遇到必须人工参与的登录或支付界面，页面弹出人机交接卡片，要求你亲手操作并点一下
Continue
按钮。你也可以随时点浏览器工具栏上的图标，把自己正在浏览的标签页借给代理，需要收回时再点一下即可。如果代理跑在另一台机器上，扩展还支持通过加密内网跨电脑连过去。
这套体验看起来顺滑，但在 2026 年 11 月的生态里已经不算新鲜事。让 AI
接管你日常打开的浏览器，市面上早就有好几款成熟工具，不少通过模型上下文协议
MCP 这套通用接口把 AI 和浏览器连起来。

Browse 仓库创建于 2026 年 10

0.1.0 这次用 AI 动的大手术。
60 美元重写了什么，又留下了什么
老版 Browse 基于 Node.js 和 Playwright 实现，打包大小在 53 到 64 MB
之间，运行时往往占一两百 MB
内存。对于一个要长期驻留在后台的小程序来说，这个开销太重了。团队想把它压成一个几
MB 的原生程序，把命令行、后台中继和 MCP
接口整合进去，同时无缝兼容已有的浏览器扩展。
11 月 15 日，
第 264
号拉取请求
合并落地，新增近 4.2
万行代码（旧版代码先留在仓库里做对照）。
The New
Stack 报道
说，Dax Raad 用 Claude Opus 当主程序员、DeepSeek
当子代理，整个重写只花了 60 美元。按团队自测，改完之后单个 Rust
二进制文件缩到 4.3 到 5.6 MB，每个连接的内存占用从大约 190 MB 降到 5.6
MB。
旧版 Node 加 Playwright 重栈与新版 Rust
加 QuickJS 轻量架构及双面工具接口对比
官方宣称内存降了 25 倍、体积缩了 23
倍，这组概括数字目前还没有外部独立复测。对比作者自己贴出的明细会发现，体积从
53 到 64 MB 压到 4.3 到 5.6
MB，大概是十几倍的降幅；中继服务内存则是拿刚启动占 6 MB 的 Rust
版本，去对比连续运行 6 天涨到 353 MB 的老 Node
进程，后者明显混进了长跑后的内存膨胀。不过从百兆级压到几兆级，体感确实轻了很多。
在
Rust
架构设计文档
里能看到，这次重写换掉了 Node 和 Playwright
运行时本身，同时也砍掉了时区与语言环境模拟以及文件下载工具，但并没有完全放弃
Playwright 的代码。为了保证识别网页按钮和页面结构的准确度，团队继续借用
Playwright
原本插进网页里的那段开源代码，省去了从零造一套识别逻辑的麻烦。同时，为了让其他编程代理仍能用脚本批量操作网页，Rust
程序里内嵌了一个轻量级 JavaScript 引擎 QuickJS。
相比换语言，这次重构里有两个接口设计更有参考价值。第一个是看客户端给菜单。OpenCode
习惯自己写逻辑拼装细粒度操作，后台程序认出它连进来，就会提供打开网页、点击、填表、截屏等二十多个独立工具。换成
Claude Code、Codex 或 Cursor
连进来，后台程序会自动收起这堆零碎工具，只留状态查询、标签页管理和一个
execute
脚本工具。多步网页操作交给内嵌的 QuickJS
一次跑完，不用把几十个工具的说明反复塞进模型的对话窗口。
第二个是砍掉抽象的会话概念，改用标签页 ID
当唯一标识。以前很多浏览器工具要先建会话再去管页面，状态容易乱。新版里打开网页直接返回一个标签页
ID，后面点击、截屏、关页面全传这个 ID，甚至能给常用页面起固定别名，比如
work-mail
。域名白名单、只读限制和标签分组，全都能干净利落地绑在单个标签页上。
写代码只要 60
美元，后面的代价藏在哪里
60 美元买来近 4.2
万行能跑的代码确实便宜，但这是写代码的钱，不是长期维护的钱。v0.1.0 在 11
月 16 日上线，不到两天团队就连发到了
v0.1.5。翻看发版后几天的故障记录，能看到不少典型的 AI
重写边界漏洞。有人敲
--help
想看帮助说明，程序竟然直接开始更新、配对和重启；文档里写明的一项前台窗口开关在
Rust 版压根没接上，记录网络请求时，短于 16
个字符的敏感查询参数也会泄漏进响应数据。
更特别的是，Browse
在项目说明里明确写着，团队不接受外部贡献者的代码合并请求，大家只管提问题单，团队的
AI 代理会很快修复。短期看响应确实快，但把 Playwright 换掉意味着未来
Chrome
升级接口、反检测策略变化或者底层协议出新坑，都得由这个小团队和它的 AI
代理自己扛。
比功能上的小毛病更令人不安的，是它运行在真正的浏览器里面。Browse
驱动的 Chrome 是你已经登录了邮箱、代码托管网站和支付网站的
Chrome，如果里面有一个网页藏了恶意提示词来诱导代理，后果会比在沙箱环境里严重得多。
OpenCode Browse
护栏能拦住的操作、页面脚本绕过路径以及默认每小时静默自更新的信任面
一位用户在
第
306
号问题单
里追问只读模式到底能防住多少，团队据此改写了安全文档。文档坦诚说明，只读模式只拦住模拟点击和输入这类常规操作，排查时还发现之前连下拉选择和文件上传都漏拦了，事后才补上。只要允许执行网页脚本，代理在只读模式下照样能读数据、点按钮和发请求；域名白名单也只管住主页面跳转，拦不住内嵌页面和网页自己发出的后台请求。
在
Hacker
News
上获得三百多赞的讨论帖
里，不少开发者对这套做法表达了强烈戒心，核心担忧就是代理同时握着你的登录账号、逛着陌生网页，还能往外发数据。项目说明里还藏着一处容易忽略的细节：Browse
的后台程序默认开启自动更新，每次启动和随后每小时都会检查官方发布服务，发现新版本就直接下载替换本地程序。就算下载带了文件校验，也可以手动关掉，但一个拿着
Chrome
调试器高权限的程序默认静默更新，等于把整个浏览器的安全直接押在了发布服务器上。
想学它重写，或者想现在就用，该怎么选
如果你正在纠结要不要学 OpenCode，用 AI
把项目的重框架重写成轻量原生程序，Browse 是一个很诚实的参考样本。AI
确实把重写轻量底层代码的门槛打下来了，花几十美元就能从重框架里抽出一小块核心功能自己实现。但前提是你能接受后续的高频修补，也有精力长期跟进上游生态的兼容性变化。如果团队本来就没人力维护底层协议，省下这几十美元买来的可能是持续不断的技术债。
如果你只想今天就让手头的 AI
编程助手在网页上干点活，可以根据自己的习惯来做选择：
追求省上下文、喜欢纯命令行工作流：优先看看 Vercel 的
agent-browser
，本身是 Rust 原生，靠简洁的命令行交互省掉大片
MCP 工具的繁琐定义。
追求大厂背书和标准调试能力：可以用微软的 Playwright MCP，或者 Google
的 Chrome DevTools
MCP，两个项目都有几万星标，官方维护链路也更清晰。
频繁需要人机交接登录、临时借出标签页，或者想通过 Tailscale
这类加密内网让远程机器上的代理操控本机浏览器：OpenCode Browse
的交互细节目前确实方便，单文件部署也够轻。
不论最后选哪一款工具，有一条底线要守住：不要把工具自带的只读模式或域名白名单当成安全隔离墙。Browse
的作者也在
第
286 号问题单
里建议，如果不想让代理接触日常环境，最好另外配一个干净的
Chrome
配置文件专门配对。把网银、主邮箱和核心后台物理隔开，只把允许代理操作的测试账号放进那个独立窗口里，同时顺手关掉默认自动更新。这样既能减少空白浏览器频频触发验证的麻烦，又能把日常核心账号和代理操作隔离开来。

items.text: innei published: AI 时代的审美赤字：当人人都能做出一个 App
items.title: AI 时代的审美赤字：当人人都能做出一个 App
items.content:
A little over half a year ago, I wrote an essay reflecting on this topic: "
The Efficiency Paradox of the AI Era: When Greater Productivity Only Leaves Us Exhausted
." Back then, I asked: in the age of AI, when productivity was supposed to be liberated, why is everyone feeling more exhausted than ever?
Over the past half-year, this trend has become increasingly obvious.
Deep, focused mental work has increasingly fractured into constant context switching across multiple projects.
It feels like we have all developed ADHD in this era, struggling to stay focused on any single thing for long.
And the more capable models become, the worse it gets: we rarely work on just one thing anymore; instead, we juggle several concurrently.
Most people are the same way, running multiple side projects at once. Building things has become almost trivial—you can easily crank out several in a single day.
On top of that, the breakneck pace of AI has made us deeply dependent on it. Now, even just kicking off a new project requires an assist from AI.
"Building It" Doesn't Mean Skill
Model progress over the past half-year has been blistering—GPT 5.4 is already an eight-month-old model.
Meanwhile, Chinese models have been playing catch-up, and by now they are at least on par with GPT 5.4. Just a few months ago, people were still debating whether hitting 5.4 would be enough to be satisfied.
With models as capable as they are now, technical barriers have largely vanished, and what people jokingly call "wishful programming"—prompting an app into existence—has become all the rage. Even a complete novice can build an app that basically meets requirements, though it might not be very good to use.
To be fair, the rapid rise of AI has let more people experience the joy of building software and create tools that help their daily lives or work—and that is genuinely meaningful.
But churning out endless garbage apps purely for hype, trend-chasing, and plagiarism is both shameful and sad.
"Building It Well" Doesn't Mean It's Valuable
In this environment, design and usability still matter immensely to me. An outsider might not grasp design philosophy or have much aesthetic sense. And among the flood of AI-generated apps everywhere, the vast majority are simply garbage.
This breakneck pace of iteration completely bypasses traditional development workflows. Design is no longer an upfront requirement in an AI workflow; it might even be outsourced entirely to whatever taste the model has. Does that mean design no longer matters?
Even apps from top-tier Chinese tech giants can leave you deeply skeptical of their aesthetics once you try them. Take Tencent's Work Buddy: daily active users have already topped 10 million, yet when I opened it with a sense of reverence, taking in its UI, visual texture, and usability, all I could call it was garbage.
Granted, perhaps that is because I consider myself a design engineer and have a heightened sensitivity to UI details.
In a climate like this, have people simply stopped caring about whether software is intuitive and beautiful?
Most users do not care about this at all. Even if the UI is hideous, the UX is clumsy, and performance is completely ignored—so long as it barely works, many users have begun to compromise, or just stopped caring altogether in this AI wave. As long as it gets their work done and delivers what they want, that is all that matters.
Examples like this are everywhere. With so many apps, you have no idea why the interface is so ugly or what the software is even supposed to help you do, yet it still manages to blow up with insane hype in this climate.
When total novices who know nothing about software engineering, architecture, or design can use marketing tactics to churn out a completely pointless piece of garbage, I find that a tragedy of our era.
Meanwhile, craftsmen who tirelessly polish a product, pouring in genuine ideas, design sensibility, and intuitive usability, get neither the recognition nor the respect they deserve—buried and forgotten simply because their growth tactics fell short. That, too, is a tragedy.
In an era like this, does it even make sense to build a product with care anymore?
The other end takes the exact same shape: in products, aesthetics are pushed behind whether something can be built at all; in models, the top-tier capabilities are consolidating into just a few companies. You have more and more to choose from, but fewer and fewer things that are actually good.
"The Best" Doesn't Mean It's Yours
Once you have used frontier models, though, your appetite is endless. Looking back, even 5.4, as the cutting-edge model of its time, was more than capable of handling most of our daily work—and today, domestic Chinese models have long surpassed that benchmark.
Constrained by compute and tightening US export controls, domestic models still face an uphill battle against America's frontier. The window to catch up is shrinking, and the frontier is moving at breakneck speed—releasing a new generation every month is considered slow, and competing labs sometimes drop two in a single month. Naturally, everyone still wants to use the most advanced models, but here in China, actually using them is only getting harder.
Among frontier model labs, OpenAI has been relatively consumer-friendly and less restrictive with regional geoblocking, but its flagship models are noticeably falling behind Anthropic's. That strikes me as a sad state of affairs. In the closed-source space, Anthropic essentially stands alone at the top right now; while Gemini and OpenAI keep trying to close the distance, the gap still feels immense.
And Anthropic happens to be a deeply anti-human organization. It feels like they just want to play dictator in the AI era, wishing nobody else would make models unless it fits the utopian society they want to construct—which is why they don't want open-weight models to evolve.

Hello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!
In
part 1
, I sent a fixed
MEOW
identifier from an Android screen to a Linux receiver. In this part, I use the same ReconCat interface and gray signal area to send a JSON snapshot made from Android Build fields. The user taps
Meow! ♥️
to start; the C receiver recovers the text, checks it, and saves it as JSON.
Part 1
already confirmed the physical Android-screen-to-ThinkPad-camera-to-Linux path: the camera recording decoded the
59
-second
MEOW
frame, passed CRC
0x0ead
, and printed
Meow-meow!
. This part expands the payload to the Build JSON and uses a shorter half-bit to keep the transfer practical, so that longer frame still needs its own complete camera decode.
The snapshot contains manufacturer, model, device, brand, hardware, board, build type, primary ABI, and Android SDK level, matching the fields in my DSP recon PoC. The app requests no Android permissions and declares no
INTERNET
permission. For simplicity of PoC, it does not read a serial number, IMEI, Android ID, location, contacts, or files.
the channel and concept
The transmitter and receiver are:

*
-> JSON -> Manchester frame -> screen brightness
|
v

in
C -> C decoder -> JSON file
The gray patch remains in the same place in the interface. The cat, plot, title, and button stay visible; only the patch carries the timed data. The Linux pipeline no longer needs a manually chosen crop rectangle. FFmpeg decodes the video and produces
640x480
grayscale frames; a small C program averages a fixed
48x48
region at the center of each frame and passes one sample per frame to the receiver.
The phone must be positioned so that the gray patch itself covers the camera image’s center. Centering the phone body is not enough if the patch falls outside that central square.

Meow! ♥️

The payload is UTF-8 JSON and is limited to
256
bytes. If the current values exceed that limit, the app stops before transmitting. The frame is:
AA AA AA AA D3 91 | length
(
16-bit BE
)
| UTF-8 JSON | XOR
(
JSON
)
| CRC32
(
32-bit BE
)
preamble +
sync
Bytes are sent most significant bit first. CRC32/IEEE covers the two length bytes, JSON and XOR byte; the receiver checks both XOR and CRC32 before writing the output file. CRC detects accidental corruption. It does not authenticate or encrypt the data.
mathematical model and timing
The Android app selects a gray level \(u(t)\in\{80,128,176\}\). Gray \(128\) is the idle and guard level. Manchester bits use levels 80 and 176:
bit 0: 80 -> 176
bit 1: 176 -> 80
167 ms per half-bit
Let the grayscale camera frame be \(I_k(x,y)\), and let \(R\) be the 48 by 48 square at its center. The C sampler turns each video frame into one value:
\[z_k = \frac{1}{\lvert R\rvert}\sum_{(x,y)\in R} I_k(x,y), \qquad \lvert R\rvert=48^2.\]
For a transmitted bit, the receiver averages samples from the central 60 percent of each half and computes
\[D_i = \bar z_{i,0} - \bar z_{i,1}.\]
With the mapping above, \(D_i\) is positive for bit
1
and negative for bit
0
. If the noiseless light and dark means differ by \(\Delta\) and the error in each half-window is bounded by \(\eta\), then the decision sign is preserved when \(\Delta>2\eta\). This implementation also rejects a pair when \(\lvert D_i\rvert\) is below 6 gray levels, so a sufficient condition for acceptance with the correct sign is
\[\Delta > 6 + 2\eta.\]
This is a sufficient condition for the decoder’s decision, not a measurement of my ThinkPad camera. Part 1 decoded the physical 250 ms frame with an estimated 0.2490 s half-bit. This part uses 167 ms halves, so the new timing and longer frame must be checked against a fresh camera recording.
The camera stream is normalized to \(f_s=30\) samples per second. With a half-bit duration \(T_h=0.167\,\mathrm{s}\), the nominal number of samples per half is
\[N_h = f_s T_h = 30 \cdot 0.167 \approx 5.01.\]
The receiver searches half-bit durations from 4.70 through 5.30 samples and scans the start phase one sample at a time. It averages the central 60 percent of each half to avoid the transition. A sufficient timing condition for those windows to remain inside the transmitted halves is
\[\lvert e_j\rvert + \frac{T_e}{2} + T_r + T_d < 0.2 T_h = 33.4\text{ ms},\]
where \(e_j\) is the sample-center error, \(T_e\) is camera exposure, \(T_r\) bounds display response, and \(T_d\) includes capture and resampling error. The implementation searches a constant-rate range; it does not read the camera’s exposure or prove that this inequality holds. That is why the webcam recording is part of the experiment.
For a JSON payload of \(L\) bytes, a frame contains \(N=L+13\) bytes: six preamble/sync bytes, two length bytes, \(L\) payload bytes, one XOR byte and four CRC bytes. Each byte has \(16\) Manchester half-bits. With five seconds of leading guard and two seconds of trailing guard, the transmission duration is
\[\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{total}} &= 7 + 16(L+13)T_h \\
&= 7 + 2.672(L+13)\ \mathrm{s}.
\end{aligned}\]
The payload limit of
256
bytes gives a maximum frame duration of
725.768
seconds. The app calculates and displays the duration for the actual device snapshot when transmission starts. The raw and useful payload rates are
\[\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{raw}} &= \frac{1}{2T_h} \approx 2.99\text{ bits/s}, \\
R_{\mathrm{useful}} &= \frac{8L}{T_{\mathrm{total}}}.
\end{aligned}\]
CRC32/IEEE uses the reflected polynomial
0xedb88320
, initial value
0xffffffff
and final XOR
0xffffffff
. A standard check value for ASCII
123456789
is
0xcbf43926
. The JSON data is accepted only if both the XOR and CRC32 match.
